title: SQL Operators: Arithmetic, Comparison, Logical and Concatenation
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and behaviour of SQL Operators: Arithmetic, Comparison, Logical and Concatenation.
Write SQLite-compatible SQL for the topic or a clearly labelled equivalent.
Predict result rows using the lesson's sample data.
Identify dialect limitations, NULL behaviour and common errors.
Apply the topic to a practical data task.

understand.concept: SQL operators combine values and expressions or test conditions. Common groups include arithmetic, comparison, logical, membership, range, pattern and concatenation operators. Operator precedence and supported symbols vary by DBMS, so parentheses improve clarity.
understand.whyItMatters: Operators make queries useful for calculations, filtering, comparisons and combining text values.
understand.analogy: Think of a SQL query as a carefully specified instruction for selecting or shaping rows in a database.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model SQL evaluation order, transaction guarantees, NULL logic or DBMS-specific implementation details.

explain.narrative:
## Operator groups
Arithmetic: `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%` (remainder in SQLite). Comparison: `=`, `<>`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`. Logical: `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`. Other common predicates include `IN`, `BETWEEN`, `LIKE` and `IS NULL`. SQLite concatenates text with `||`; other DBMS products may use different concatenation operators or functions. Use parentheses to make mixed conditions unambiguous.

## Common mistakes
- Assuming syntax is identical across all database engines.
- Omitting explicit column lists when moving data.
- Ignoring NULL, constraints or result ordering.
- Treating a documented dialect example as executable SQLite syntax.

## Best practices
Use explicit columns, test against the target DBMS/version, keep setup scripts repeatable, and verify results with SELECT queries.

examples.title: Calculate line totals with arithmetic operators
examples.explanation: Multiplication and subtraction calculate totals; parentheses can clarify more complex formulas.

examples.title: Filter with comparison operators
examples.explanation: Comparison operators produce conditions that can be combined in WHERE.

examples.title: Combine logical conditions with parentheses
examples.explanation: Parentheses make the intended OR group evaluate before the AND condition.

examples.title: Concatenate text with SQLite's operator
examples.explanation: SQLite uses || for string concatenation; CONCAT() or other syntax may be preferred in other DBMS products.

examples.title: Use remainder and range predicates
examples.explanation: BETWEEN is inclusive, and % returns the remainder in SQLite; both conditions must be true.

practise.guidedTask: Run the five examples in order. Before each run, predict the result and explain how SQL Operators: Arithmetic, Comparison, Logical and Concatenation affects it.
practise.independentTask: Create your own small dataset and write three new queries using SQL Operators: Arithmetic, Comparison, Logical and Concatenation. Include one boundary case and document the expected output.
hints: Read the target DBMS syntax notes before running an example.

Use ORDER BY when the display order matters.
Compare the returned rows with your prediction after execution.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes SQLite text concatenation?
options: It concatenates text values in SQLite
It performs numeric division
It tests whether a value is NULL
It creates a new table
questions.answer: It concatenates text values in SQLite
questions.explanation: SQLite uses the || operator for text concatenation.

questions.prompt: Which practice is safest for this topic?
options: Name columns explicitly and verify dialect support
Assume all SQL dialects use identical syntax
Ignore NULL and constraint behaviour
Rely on implicit row order
questions.answer: Name columns explicitly and verify dialect support
questions.explanation: Explicit columns, dialect checks and clear assumptions make SQL predictable.

questions.prompt: What should a learner check before relying on this feature?
options: The target DBMS and its supported syntax
Only the browser screen size
The name of the SQL file
Whether the query has uppercase keywords
questions.answer: The target DBMS and its supported syntax
questions.explanation: SQL syntax and behaviour can vary between database engines and versions.

questions.prompt: Which statement about query results is correct?
options: A result should be ordered explicitly when order matters
Rows are always returned in insertion order
Aliases change the stored source table
Comments alter the result set
questions.answer: A result should be ordered explicitly when order matters
questions.explanation: Without ORDER BY, SQL does not guarantee a particular result order.
